lessons.title: Grain: what one row means
lessons.hook: Almost every wrong number in SQL comes from the same mistake, and it is not a syntax error. It is joining two tables that count different things and never deciding which one a row is supposed to be.
objectives: State the grain of a table in one sentence before writing a query against it
Predict what a join does to the grain before running it
Recognise the symptom of a grain mistake in a result set
key_points: The grain of a table is what exactly one row represents — 'one loan', 'one scheduled payment', 'one borrower'.
In the lending dataset: borrowers is one row per borrower, loans is one row per loan, payments is one row per scheduled payment on a loan.
A join changes the grain whenever the right-hand side has more than one matching row. Joining loans to payments produces one row per payment, not per loan.
Once the grain has changed, any column from the left table repeats. Summing it counts the same value once per matching row on the right.
The classic symptom is a total that is too large by roughly the average number of child rows — not a random wrong number, an inflated one.
The fix is to aggregate to the grain you want before joining, or to aggregate after joining using a key that is unique at the target grain (COUNT DISTINCT, or SUM over a pre-aggregated subquery).
Saying the grain out loud before writing the query is the single habit that prevents this class of error.

example.caption: loans has 24 rows. Joining it to payments returns 72 — one per payment. Watch what that does to a sum of principal.
example.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_returned, ROUND(SUM(l.principal), 2) AS principal_sum FROM loans l JOIN payments p ON p.loan_id = l.loan_id
example.body: Compare that principal_sum against the honest one: SELECT ROUND(SUM(principal),2) FROM loans. The join version is inflated because each loan's principal is counted once per payment attached to it.

misconceptions.claim: A LEFT JOIN is safe because it keeps all the left rows.
misconceptions.correction: LEFT JOIN protects you from losing rows, not from gaining them. If the right table has three matches, the left row appears three times.

misconceptions.claim: SELECT DISTINCT will fix a duplicated join.
misconceptions.correction: It removes identical rows, which hides the symptom without fixing the grain. If two payments differ, the loan row still appears twice with different payment columns.

misconceptions.claim: COUNT(*) tells you how many loans there are.
misconceptions.correction: It tells you how many rows the query produced. After a fan-out join those are different numbers.

lessons.interview_angle: Usually arrives as 'this revenue number looks too high, what would you check'. The answer that lands is naming the grain of each table and where the join changed it — before touching the query.

lessons.title: NULL is not a value
lessons.hook: NULL means 'unknown', and unknown behaves differently from every other value in SQL. Filters silently drop rows, comparisons return neither true nor false, and aggregate functions quietly disagree with each other.
objectives: Predict which rows a WHERE clause drops when a column is nullable
Choose between COUNT(*), COUNT(col) and SUM(CASE...) deliberately
Write a null-safe comparison
key_points: SQL uses three-valued logic: TRUE, FALSE and UNKNOWN. Any comparison with NULL returns UNKNOWN.
WHERE keeps only rows where the predicate is TRUE. UNKNOWN rows are dropped, so `WHERE paid_at != '2024-01-01'` excludes rows where paid_at is NULL.
NULL = NULL is UNKNOWN, not TRUE. Use IS NULL and IS NOT NULL, which are the only operators that test for it.
COUNT(*) counts rows. COUNT(column) counts non-null values in that column. The gap between them is the number of NULLs.
SUM, AVG and MAX skip NULLs. AVG in particular divides by the count of non-null values, not by the row count — so AVG is not SUM/COUNT(*).
In the lending dataset, payments.paid_at is NULL for a payment that has not been made. That single column is how you find delinquency.
NOT IN with a subquery that can return NULL returns no rows at all, because the comparison is UNKNOWN for every candidate. NOT EXISTS does not have this problem.

example.caption: Three ways of counting payments that disagree, and the NULL that explains why.
example.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS all_payments, COUNT(paid_at) AS paid, COUNT(*) - COUNT(paid_at) AS unpaid FROM payments
example.body: COUNT(*) counts every scheduled payment; COUNT(paid_at) counts only the ones actually made. The difference is the delinquency, and it exists only because paid_at is nullable.

misconceptions.claim: `WHERE status != 'closed'` returns everything that is not closed.
misconceptions.correction: It returns everything not closed AND not null. Rows with a null status vanish, which is usually not what was meant.

misconceptions.claim: AVG(x) is the same as SUM(x)/COUNT(*).
misconceptions.correction: AVG divides by COUNT(x), which excludes nulls. If a fifth of your values are null, the two differ by a fifth.

misconceptions.claim: NULL = NULL is true, because they are both null.
misconceptions.correction: It is UNKNOWN. Two unknowns are not known to be equal — that is what unknown means.

lessons.interview_angle: Often a trap inside a larger question: a filter on a nullable column that quietly changes the population. Saying 'this drops the nulls, is that intended' is the whole answer.

lessons.title: Joins, and what each one is for
lessons.hook: There are four joins worth knowing and two patterns built out of them. Most people know INNER and LEFT and reach for them for everything, which is why semi-join and anti-join questions separate candidates.
objectives: Choose the join that matches the question being asked
Write a semi-join and an anti-join without duplicating rows
Explain why a filter in ON differs from the same filter in WHERE
key_points: INNER JOIN keeps rows that match on both sides. LEFT JOIN keeps every left row and fills the right with NULLs when there is no match.
A semi-join answers 'which left rows have at least one match' without bringing the right columns across. EXISTS is the direct way to write it and it cannot change the grain.
An anti-join answers 'which left rows have no match'. NOT EXISTS is the safe form; LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.key IS NULL is the same thing written longer.

A filter on the right table placed in the ON clause of a LEFT JOIN is applied before the join, so non-matching left rows survive with NULLs. The same filter in WHERE is applied after, which silently turns the LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN.
CROSS JOIN produces every combination. It is occasionally what you want — generating a date spine, for instance — and is otherwise a missing join condition.
Joining on a non-unique key on both sides multiplies rows: three matches on the left and two on the right produce six rows.

example.caption: Anti-join: borrowers who have never missed a payment. Six of the sixteen, and not one of them can be duplicated by the query.
example.sql: SELECT b.borrower_id, b.fico_band, b.state_code FROM borrowers b WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM loans l JOIN payments p ON p.loan_id = l.loan_id WHERE l.borrower_id = b.borrower_id AND p.paid_at IS NULL)
example.body: Note what NOT EXISTS buys here. The inner query joins loans to payments and fans out to many rows per borrower — but because the outer query only asks whether any exist, the borrower appears once or not at all. Writing this as a LEFT JOIN would need a DISTINCT to undo the fan-out, and NOT IN would return nothing at all if any borrower_id in the subquery were NULL.

misconceptions.claim: LEFT JOIN with a WHERE on the right table still keeps all left rows.
misconceptions.correction: It does not. WHERE runs after the join, and NULL fails almost every predicate, so unmatched left rows are filtered out. Put the condition in ON instead.

misconceptions.claim: NOT IN and NOT EXISTS are interchangeable.
misconceptions.correction: If the subquery returns even one NULL, NOT IN returns nothing at all, because every comparison becomes UNKNOWN. NOT EXISTS is unaffected.

lessons.interview_angle: 'Find the customers who did X but not Y' is an anti-join question and is extremely common. Reaching for NOT EXISTS rather than a LEFT JOIN with an IS NULL filter reads as fluency.

lessons.title: Aggregation changes the grain on purpose
lessons.hook: GROUP BY is the one operation that changes grain deliberately. Understanding it as a grain change rather than as 'grouping' makes HAVING, filtered aggregates and double-counting all obvious.
objectives: Describe what GROUP BY does to the grain of a result
Choose between WHERE and HAVING correctly
Aggregate conditionally without a subquery
key_points: GROUP BY collapses many rows into one per distinct combination of the grouping columns. The output grain is exactly those columns.
Every selected column must either be in the GROUP BY or inside an aggregate, because anything else has no single value at the new grain.
WHERE filters rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after. A filter that mentions an aggregate can only go in HAVING; a filter on a raw column belongs in WHERE, where it is cheaper.
SUM(CASE WHEN condition THEN value END) is conditional aggregation — it computes a filtered measure alongside an unfiltered one in a single pass, with no subquery.
COUNT(DISTINCT x) counts unique values and is the usual repair when a join has already fanned the rows out.
Aggregating after a fan-out join double-counts. Aggregate to the target grain first, then join, whenever the measure comes from the parent table.

example.caption: Paid and unpaid amounts per loan, in one pass, using conditional aggregation.
example.sql: SELECT l.loan_id, l.product, ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN p.paid_at IS NOT NULL THEN p.amount ELSE 0 END), 2) AS paid, ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN p.paid_at IS NULL THEN p.amount ELSE 0 END), 2) AS outstanding FROM loans l JOIN payments p ON p.loan_id = l.loan_id GROUP BY l.loan_id, l.product ORDER BY outstanding DESC LIMIT 8
example.body: The grain of the result is one row per loan, restored by the GROUP BY after the join fanned it out to one row per payment.

misconceptions.claim: HAVING is just WHERE for GROUP BY queries.
misconceptions.correction: HAVING runs after aggregation and can see aggregates; WHERE runs before and cannot. Putting a raw-column filter in HAVING works but scans more rows than it needs to.

misconceptions.claim: COUNT(DISTINCT id) is a good way to fix double counting.
misconceptions.correction: It fixes counts, not sums. If a join duplicated rows, SUM(amount) is still wrong and no DISTINCT will repair it — you have to fix the grain.

lessons.interview_angle: Conditional aggregation is the thing to reach for when asked for 'paid vs unpaid in one result'. Writing it as two subqueries joined together works and reads as less fluent.

lessons.title: Window functions: aggregate without collapsing
lessons.hook: A window function computes across a set of rows and keeps every row. That single property answers running totals, rankings, per-group comparisons and period-over-period change — the questions GROUP BY cannot answer without a self-join.
objectives: Use OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...) correctly
Choose between ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK
Explain what a frame is and when the default one bites
key_points: A window function is computed over a set of rows related to the current row, and does not reduce the number of rows returned.
PARTITION BY divides the rows into independent groups. ORDER BY inside OVER decides the order within each partition, which is what makes running totals and lag possible.
ROW_NUMBER always produces distinct consecutive integers. RANK leaves gaps after ties. DENSE_RANK does not leave gaps. Choosing the wrong one is a common silent bug in 'top N per group'.

The frame defines which rows of the partition the function sees. With ORDER BY present the default frame is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW — a running total. Without ORDER BY it is the whole partition.
That default frame with RANGE treats tied ORDER BY values as one unit, which can include rows you expected to be excluded. ROWS BETWEEN is the explicit and usually intended form.
LAG and LEAD read the previous or next row in the partition, which is how period-over-period change is written without a self-join.
Window functions run after WHERE and GROUP BY, so you cannot filter on one in WHERE. Wrap it in a subquery or CTE and filter outside — that is the standard 'top N per group' shape.

example.caption: Running paid total per loan, in payment order — a window function keeping every row.
example.sql: SELECT loan_id, due_at, amount, ROUND(SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY loan_id ORDER BY due_at ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS running_total FROM payments ORDER BY loan_id, due_at LIMIT 10
example.body: PARTITION BY restarts the total for each loan; ORDER BY makes 'running' meaningful; ROWS BETWEEN states the frame rather than relying on the default.

misconceptions.claim: You can filter on a window function in the WHERE clause.
misconceptions.correction: Window functions are evaluated after WHERE, so the column does not exist yet. Compute it in a CTE and filter in the outer query.

misconceptions.claim: RANK and ROW_NUMBER are interchangeable for top-N.
misconceptions.correction: With ties, RANK returns more than N rows and skips numbers. ROW_NUMBER always returns exactly N but breaks ties arbitrarily unless you order deterministically.

misconceptions.claim: The default frame does not matter.
misconceptions.correction: With ORDER BY the default is a running frame, not the whole partition — so AVG(x) OVER (ORDER BY d) is a running average, not the partition average, which surprises people constantly.

lessons.interview_angle: 'Top 3 per category' and 'month-over-month change' are the two most common SQL screening questions above the beginner level, and both are one window function. Being able to say why the filter has to move to an outer query is the part that separates answers.

lessons.title: Why a query is slow: indexes and the planner
lessons.hook: A database does not run your query, it runs a plan it chose. Knowing roughly how it chooses turns 'this is slow' from a mystery into a short list of causes.
objectives: Read a query plan well enough to find the expensive step
Say why an index helps, and when it cannot
Recognise the query shapes that defeat an index
key_points: An index is a sorted structure mapping column values to row locations, so the engine can find matching rows without reading the whole table. It costs storage and slows writes.
The planner estimates the cost of alternative plans using statistics about the data, and picks the cheapest estimate. A bad plan is usually a bad estimate, not a bad optimiser.
A full scan is not automatically wrong. When a query touches most of the table, scanning is cheaper than jumping through an index for every row.
Wrapping an indexed column in a function defeats the index: WHERE date(originated_at) = '2024-01-01' cannot use an index on originated_at, while a range condition on the raw column can.
Leading-column order matters in a composite index. An index on (a, b) helps a query filtering on a, or on a and b, but generally not one filtering on b alone.
A covering index contains every column the query needs, so the engine never touches the table itself.
EXPLAIN shows the chosen plan. The steps to look for are the ones that scan the most rows and the joins whose estimated row counts look wrong.

example.caption: The shape that defeats an index: a function wrapped around the filtered column. Both queries return the same rows; only one of them could use an index on originated_at.
example.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS matched FROM loans WHERE originated_at >= '2024-01-01' AND originated_at < '2025-01-01'
example.body: Written as substr(originated_at, 1, 4) = '2024' it returns the same count and cannot use an index, because the engine would have to compute the function for every row before it could compare. The range form leaves the column bare, so an index on it can be scanned directly. This dataset is 24 rows and will be scanned either way — the point is the shape, which is what stops being free at a million rows.

misconceptions.claim: Adding an index makes queries faster.
misconceptions.correction: It makes some reads faster and all writes slower, and only helps when the query filters or joins on the indexed column in a form the planner can use.

misconceptions.claim: A slow query means a missing index.
misconceptions.correction: It often means a fan-out join, a function on a filtered column, or statistics that are stale enough for the planner to pick badly.

lessons.interview_angle: Usually 'this dashboard query takes 40 seconds, what do you do'. The strong answer starts with reading the plan and the row counts rather than guessing at an index.

lessons.title: Tokens: the unit the model actually sees
lessons.hook: A model does not read characters and does not read words. It reads tokens, and almost every surprising behaviour — the cost of a call, why it miscounts letters, why some languages cost triple — falls out of that one fact.
objectives: Explain what a token is and why it is neither a character nor a word
Predict roughly what a piece of text costs before sending it
Say why a model struggles with character-level tasks
key_points: A token is a chunk of text from a fixed vocabulary learned before training. Common words are usually one token; rare words split into several.
Modern models use subword tokenisation, typically byte-pair encoding or a variant: start from characters and repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair until the vocabulary is full.
Subword tokenisation exists to solve two problems at once — a fixed vocabulary that never meets an unknown word, and a sequence length short enough to be tractable.
For English prose a token is roughly four characters, so about 0.75 words. That ratio is a rule of thumb, not a rule: code, JSON, names and non-Latin scripts all tokenise worse.
Billing, rate limits and the context window are all counted in tokens, not words — so the same paragraph in Hindi or Japanese can cost several times what it costs in English.
The model never sees the letters inside a token. That is why counting the r's in a word is genuinely hard for it, and why it is not a sign of poor reasoning.
Tokenisation is fixed at training time. You cannot change it with a prompt, and the same string always produces the same tokens for a given model.

example.caption: Why 'strawberry' is hard and 'the' is easy
example.body: A frequent word like 'the' is one token — the model has a single vector for it. 'strawberry' typically splits into pieces such as 'straw' and 'berry'. The model sees two chunks, not ten letters, so asking how many r's it contains is asking it to report on something it never received. Meanwhile a JSON blob full of braces, quotes and field names tokenises far worse than the same information in prose, which is a real and often-overlooked cost.

misconceptions.claim: A token is a word.
misconceptions.correction: Only for common words. Rare words, names, code and any non-English script routinely split into several tokens each.

misconceptions.claim: The model is bad at spelling because it is not smart enough.
misconceptions.correction: It is a representation problem, not a reasoning one. Character-level detail is discarded before the model ever sees the input.

misconceptions.claim: Token counts are the same across models.
misconceptions.correction: Each model family has its own vocabulary, so the same text can differ substantially in token count between them.

lessons.interview_angle: 'Why is this API call expensive' and 'why can't it count letters' are both tokenisation questions. Knowing the ~4-characters rule of thumb and that non-English costs more is the practical half.

lessons.title: Embeddings: meaning as coordinates
lessons.hook: Once text is a list of numbers positioned so that similar meanings sit close together, 'do these two sentences mean the same thing' becomes 'how far apart are they' — a question a computer can answer exactly.
objectives: Explain what an embedding is and what the distance between two of them means
Say why cosine similarity is the usual measure
Recognise when semantic search beats keyword search, and when it does not
key_points: An embedding is a fixed-length vector representing a piece of text, produced by a model trained so that semantically similar inputs land near each other.
Similarity is usually measured by cosine similarity — the angle between two vectors — rather than straight-line distance, because it compares direction and ignores magnitude.
The dimensions are learned, not designed. No single dimension means 'formality' or 'topic'; meaning is distributed across all of them, which is why an embedding cannot be read.
Embeddings are model-specific. Vectors from two different models are not comparable, and re-embedding an entire corpus is the real cost of changing model.
Semantic search finds text that means the same thing in different words; keyword search finds exact terms. Each fails where the other works — an exact product code is a keyword problem.
Hybrid retrieval combines both, and in practice usually beats either alone.
An embedding of a long document is an average of everything in it, so distinct topics blur together. That is the argument for chunking before embedding.

example.caption: Why 'how do I cancel' matches 'terminating your subscription'
example.body: Neither phrase shares a content word with the other, so keyword search scores them at zero. Their embeddings sit close because the training data contained enough examples of the two being used in the same situations. Now flip it: search for the part number 'BX-4471'. Semantic search returns a spread of plausible-looking part numbers, all wrong, with high confidence — because to an embedding model those strings genuinely are similar. Keyword search finds it instantly.

misconceptions.claim: A high cosine similarity means the two texts say the same thing.
misconceptions.correction: It means they are used in similar contexts. 'I loved it' and 'I hated it' can score high, because opposites appear in near-identical surroundings.

misconceptions.claim: You can compare embeddings from different models.
misconceptions.correction: The vector spaces are unrelated. Distances between them are meaningless.

misconceptions.claim: Embeddings replace keyword search.
misconceptions.correction: They are worse at exact identifiers, codes, names and rare terms — which is why serious systems run both.

lessons.interview_angle: Usually reached through RAG: 'how would you find the relevant documents'. Naming the failure mode — exact identifiers — is what shows you have actually run one.

lessons.title: Attention: how a model decides what matters
lessons.hook: When you read 'it' in a sentence, you look back to work out what it refers to. Attention is the model doing that for every position at once, and learning how hard to look at each one. It is the mechanism the whole transformer is built around.
objectives: Explain self-attention in terms of queries, keys and values
Say why attention replaced recurrence for long sequences
Explain where the quadratic cost comes from and what it implies
key_points: Attention lets every position in a sequence look at every other position and weight how relevant each one is to it, rather than compressing the past into a single fixed-size state.
Each position produces three vectors: a query — what am I looking for, a key — what do I offer, and a value — what I pass on if attended to.
A position's output is a weighted sum of all the values, where the weights come from comparing its query against every key and normalising through a softmax so they sum to one.
Self-attention means the queries, keys and values all come from the same sequence — the sentence attending to itself. That is what resolves 'it' to a noun forty words earlier.
Multi-head attention runs several attention operations in parallel on different learned projections, so one head can track syntax while another tracks reference.
Because every position compares against every other, cost grows with the square of sequence length. Doubling the context quadruples the work.
Attention has no inherent notion of order — it sees a set, not a sequence — so position must be added separately through positional encoding.

This replaced recurrent models, which had to carry information forward step by step and lost it over distance. The 2017 paper introducing the transformer is titled 'Attention Is All You Need' for that reason.

example.caption: 'The loan was denied because it was incomplete' — what does 'it' attend to?
example.body: A recurrent model reads left to right, compressing everything seen so far into one state; by the time it reaches 'it', 'loan' and 'application' are blurred together in that state. Self-attention instead lets the position holding 'it' compare directly against every earlier position and put most of its weight on the one that resolves the reference. Nothing was compressed and nothing had to survive a journey — which is exactly why long-range dependencies stopped being the hard case.

misconceptions.claim: Attention weights are an explanation of the model's reasoning.
misconceptions.correction: They show where information was drawn from, not why an output was produced. Treating them as explanations is a well-known overreach.

misconceptions.claim: Transformers process text sequentially like earlier models.
misconceptions.correction: All positions are processed in parallel. That parallelism is what made training at this scale practical, and it is why order has to be injected separately.

misconceptions.claim: A bigger context window is free.
misconceptions.correction: Attention cost is quadratic in length, which is why long context is expensive and why most efficiency research targets exactly this.

lessons.interview_angle: 'Explain attention' is a standard opener for any AI-adjacent role. Queries, keys and values plus the quadratic cost is a complete answer; reciting the softmax formula without the intuition is not.

lessons.title: Prompting: the cheapest place to change behaviour
lessons.hook: There are three ways to change what a model does — change the input, change what it can see, or change its weights. Prompting is the first, and it is instant, reversible and free, which is why it should almost always be tried first.
objectives: Structure a prompt so the important instruction is actually followed
Choose between zero-shot, few-shot and decomposition
Say what a prompt fundamentally cannot fix
key_points: Prompting shapes behaviour through the input alone, leaving the weights untouched. It is the cheapest of the three levers and the only one that is instantly reversible.
Being specific about the task, the format and the audience does more than any phrasing trick. Most apparent capability gaps are underspecified requests.
Few-shot prompting — showing worked examples in the prompt — teaches format and edge-case handling far more reliably than describing them in prose.
Asking for reasoning before the answer improves multi-step tasks, because the model conditions each token on what it has already produced; an answer given first cannot be reasoned toward.
Decomposing a hard task into several calls usually beats one elaborate prompt, and each step becomes separately testable.
Constraining the output shape — a schema, an enum, a strict JSON format — removes a whole class of parsing failure and makes the result checkable.
A prompt cannot supply a fact the model was never given. If the answer depends on current or private information, no rewording produces it — that is what retrieval is for.
Prompts are brittle across models and across versions. What works on one model is a starting point on another, not a solution.

example.caption: The same request, twice
example.body: 'Summarise this document' gives you an unpredictable length in an unpredictable register. 'In three bullet points, each under twenty words, summarise what this loan file says about the borrower's income — for a credit analyst deciding whether to request more documentation' gives you something usable. Nothing clever happened. The task, the format, the audience and the decision were named, and each one removed a degree of freedom the model would otherwise have guessed at.

misconceptions.claim: There are magic phrases that unlock better performance.
misconceptions.correction: Specificity, examples and structure do the work. Incantations mostly move results within noise.

misconceptions.claim: A longer prompt is a better prompt.
misconceptions.correction: Filling the window dilutes the material that matters; relevant content competes with everything else for attention.

misconceptions.claim: If prompting fails, fine-tune.
misconceptions.correction: Usually the next step is retrieval. Fine-tuning teaches form and style; it is a poor and expensive way to teach facts.

lessons.interview_angle: Often 'how would you improve this output'. The strong answer names the ladder — prompt, then retrieval, then fine-tuning — and explains why you climb it in that order.

lessons.title: RAG: giving the model the page before it answers
lessons.hook: A model's weights are frozen at training time and carry no citation. Retrieval puts a search step in front of generation so the answer is written from documents you chose — which changes where the failure lives rather than removing it.
objectives: Describe the retrieval pipeline end to end
Explain why chunking strategy decides retrieval quality
Say how you would evaluate a RAG system, and what you would measure separately
key_points: Retrieval-augmented generation retrieves relevant documents for a query and places them in the prompt, so the answer is grounded in supplied text rather than in memorised weights.
It addresses three limits at once: knowledge frozen at training time, no access to private data, and no citation for what is asserted.
Documents are split into chunks before embedding, because an embedding of a long document averages everything in it and blurs distinct topics together.

Chunking strategy is the highest-leverage decision in the pipeline. Too small and a chunk loses the context that made it meaningful; too large and retrieval returns mostly irrelevant text. Overlapping chunks reduce the risk of splitting an answer in half.
Reranking is a second, more expensive pass over the top candidates from cheap vector search. It substantially improves precision and is often the difference between a demo and something usable.
Hybrid retrieval — vector plus keyword — beats either alone, because embeddings are weak on exact identifiers and keyword search is weak on paraphrase.
The failure mode moves rather than disappearing: retrieve the wrong passage and the model will answer confidently and fluently from it.

Retrieval and generation must be evaluated separately. If you only measure the final answer you cannot tell whether a bad answer came from bad retrieval or bad generation, and they have completely different fixes.

example.caption: Where a RAG answer actually goes wrong
example.body: A user asks about the escrow policy. The retriever returns a chunk from last year's version of the policy document, because it is textually near-identical to this year's. The generator does its job perfectly: it answers accurately from the passage it was handed. The output is fluent, confident, cites a real document, and is wrong. No amount of prompt work fixes it — the defect is upstream, in retrieval, which is precisely why the two halves get measured separately.

misconceptions.claim: RAG stops hallucination.
misconceptions.correction: It reduces invention from nothing and introduces confident answers from the wrong source. Grounding is only as good as retrieval.

misconceptions.claim: Bigger context windows make RAG unnecessary.
misconceptions.correction: Retrieval still decides what is worth putting in the window, and stuffing everything in raises cost and dilutes attention across irrelevant material.

misconceptions.claim: Chunk size is a tuning detail.
misconceptions.correction: It is the decision that most determines whether the right passage can be retrieved at all. Nothing downstream recovers from a chunk that split the answer.

lessons.interview_angle: 'How would you build a chatbot over our documentation' is a RAG question. The answers that stand out talk about chunking, hybrid retrieval, and evaluating retrieval separately from generation.

lessons.title: Evals: knowing whether a change made it better
lessons.hook: An LLM system has no unit tests in the ordinary sense — the same input can produce different valid outputs. Without a way to measure, every change is a guess, and 'it seems better' is how systems quietly get worse.
objectives: Design an eval set for a specific task
Choose between exact match, human judgement and model-as-judge
Say what a model-as-judge grader is bad at
key_points: An eval is a fixed set of inputs with a way to score outputs, run repeatedly so that a change can be compared against a known baseline rather than against an impression.
Build it from real failures. Every bug worth fixing becomes a case, which turns the suite into a regression test that grows where the system is actually weak.

Scoring methods trade off: exact match and structural checks are cheap, objective and only work for constrained outputs; human judgement is the gold standard and does not scale; a model grading a model scales and carries its own biases.
LLM-as-judge is standard practice with documented failure modes — it favours longer answers, prefers its own family's style, and is sensitive to option order in pairwise comparisons.
A judge must be validated against human labels on a sample before its scores are trusted. Without that you are measuring agreement with a model, not quality.
Component evals beat end-to-end ones for diagnosis. In a retrieval system, measure retrieval and generation separately or a regression tells you nothing about where it came from.
Non-determinism means a single run is not evidence. Fix the seed and temperature where possible, and otherwise run repeatedly and compare distributions.
Cost and latency belong in the eval alongside quality, because a change that improves answers and triples the bill is a trade-off someone has to make deliberately.

example.caption: Why the containment gate in this very app is an eval
example.body: CareerOS generates outreach email and refuses any sentence carrying a figure with no evidence claim behind it. That check runs on every generation, has a fixed pass condition, and rejects the whole message on failure. It caught the model attributing a figure of 97 to a claim that does not contain it — automatically, on a real generation, with no human reading it. That is an eval doing its job: a measurable property, checked every time, that fails loudly rather than degrading quietly.

misconceptions.claim: Eyeballing a few outputs is enough.
misconceptions.correction: It cannot detect a regression on cases you did not think to try, and it is exactly how systems get slowly worse while feeling fine.

misconceptions.claim: A model-as-judge score is objective because it is a number.
misconceptions.correction: It is a model's opinion rendered as a number, with known biases toward length and its own style. Validate it against human labels before trusting it.

misconceptions.claim: A passing eval means the system is good.
misconceptions.correction: It means the system is good on the cases you wrote. Coverage is the whole game, which is why failures should become cases.

lessons.interview_angle: 'How do you know your LLM feature works' separates people who have shipped one from people who have demoed one. Naming a real eval set, built from real failures, with retrieval measured separately, is the answer.

lessons.title: Sampling: why a sample can speak for a population
lessons.hook: Every number you report is computed from a sample, including the ones that feel like the whole population. Knowing what that costs you is the difference between a figure and a figure you can defend.
objectives: Say what a sampling distribution is
Explain why the standard error shrinks with n
Spot the sampling problem in a business metric
key_points: A statistic computed from a sample is itself a random quantity: draw a different sample and you get a different value.
The distribution of that statistic across all possible samples is the sampling distribution, and it is what all of inference is about.

The central limit theorem says the sampling distribution of a mean approaches a normal shape as the sample grows, whatever the shape of the underlying data. That is why normal-based methods work on data that is not normal.
The standard error is the standard deviation of the sampling distribution. For a mean it shrinks with the square root of n, so quadrupling the sample halves the error — precision gets expensive fast.
Sample size fixes noise, not bias. A biased sampling process gives you a precisely wrong answer, and a bigger sample makes it more precisely wrong.
Survivorship bias is the most common business version: measuring only the customers who stayed, the loans that completed, the applications that got a response.
'We used all the data' is usually false. All the data you have is a sample of all the data there could be, drawn by a process you did not design.

example.caption: Why last month's delinquency rate is a sample
example.body: Take every loan in the book and compute the share that missed a payment. That feels like a population, not a sample — you used all the rows. But the question being asked is almost never 'what happened in these rows'; it is 'what is our delinquency rate', which is about a process that will keep generating loans. This month's book is one draw from that process. It has a standard error, it will move next month without anything changing, and a swing of half a point on 200 loans is noise you should expect rather than a trend to explain.

misconceptions.claim: If I have all the data, there is no sampling error.
misconceptions.correction: Only if the question is about exactly those rows. Any question about an ongoing process treats what you have as one draw from it.

misconceptions.claim: A bigger sample fixes a bad sample.
misconceptions.correction: It shrinks the noise around a biased estimate. The bias is unchanged, so you converge confidently on the wrong number.

misconceptions.claim: The central limit theorem means my data is normal.
misconceptions.correction: It says the sampling distribution of the mean tends to normal. The data itself can be as skewed as it likes.

lessons.interview_angle: Usually arrives as 'this metric moved 3% week over week, is that real'. The answer that lands starts with how many observations it is computed from.

lessons.title: Estimation: a number with its uncertainty attached
lessons.hook: A point estimate on its own hides the only thing a decision-maker needs: how much it could move. An interval says both.
objectives: Interpret a confidence interval correctly
Choose an interval over a point estimate
Say what a wide interval is telling you
key_points: A confidence interval is built by a procedure such that, across repeated samples, a stated share of the intervals it produces would contain the true value.
The 95% refers to the procedure's long-run behaviour, not to a probability about the one interval in front of you — that interval either contains the truth or it does not.
Interval width is driven by the variability in the data and by the sample size, so a wide interval is a statement about how little the data settles the question.
An interval spanning zero, for a difference, means the data do not settle the direction of the effect. Reporting that honestly is a finding, not a failure.
Intervals answer the decision question better than p-values, because they carry the size of the effect as well as whether it is distinguishable from nothing.
Bootstrapping estimates an interval by resampling the data with replacement, which works for statistics with no clean formula — medians, ratios, custom metrics.
Always report the interval alongside the estimate. A number without one invites a precision the data does not have.

example.caption: Two forecasts, same point estimate
example.body: Two models both forecast next quarter's volume at 1,200. One says 1,150 to 1,250; the other says 600 to 1,800. The point estimate is identical and the two are not remotely the same answer — the first supports a staffing decision and the second says you do not know yet. Reporting only 1,200 makes those indistinguishable, which is how a forecast gets trusted more than it deserves.

misconceptions.claim: There is a 95% chance the true value is in this interval.
misconceptions.correction: The true value is fixed. The 95% describes how often the procedure captures it across repeated samples, which is a statement about the method.

misconceptions.claim: Overlapping intervals mean no significant difference.
misconceptions.correction: Not reliably. Two intervals can overlap while the interval for their difference excludes zero — test the difference directly.

lessons.interview_angle: 'How confident are you in that number' is an invitation to talk about intervals. Answering with a feeling rather than a range is the tell.

lessons.title: Hypothesis testing, and the errors it trades
lessons.hook: A test is a decision rule with a known false-alarm rate. Everything confusing about p-values dissolves once you see it as a rule you set in advance rather than a measurement you take afterwards.
objectives: State a null hypothesis precisely
Explain type I and type II error and what trades between them
Name why testing many things at once inflates false positives
key_points: The null hypothesis is the specific claim of 'nothing going on' that the test is built against. Vague nulls produce uninterpretable tests.
A p-value is the probability of data at least this extreme if the null were true. It is a statement about data given a hypothesis, never about the hypothesis given the data.
A type I error is rejecting a true null — a false alarm — and its rate is the threshold you chose. A type II error is failing to detect a real effect.
Lowering the threshold reduces false alarms and increases missed effects. Which error is worse is a business question, not a statistical one.
Power is the probability of detecting an effect of a given size if it is real. Low power means a null result tells you almost nothing.
Testing twenty independent things at the 5% level means one is expected to look significant by chance. Corrections such as Bonferroni or false discovery rate exist for exactly this.
Stopping as soon as the result looks significant is the same error spread over time, and it substantially inflates the false positive rate.
Statistical significance is not effect size. With a large enough sample, a difference too small to act on becomes significant.

example.caption: Why the fraud rule and the auto-reject rule need different thresholds
example.body: A screening rule that flags possible fraud for human review should tolerate false alarms: a type I error costs an analyst ten minutes. A rule that auto-declines an application cannot: the same error is a real customer turned away with no recourse. Identical statistics, opposite thresholds, and the reason is entirely about which mistake you are willing to make.

misconceptions.claim: p = 0.03 means a 3% chance the result is wrong.
misconceptions.correction: It is the probability of the data under the null, not the probability the null is true. Those are different quantities and the second needs a prior.

misconceptions.claim: A non-significant result means there is no effect.
misconceptions.correction: It means this data did not distinguish one. With low power that is expected even for real effects.

misconceptions.claim: p = 0.049 and p = 0.051 are different findings.
misconceptions.correction: They are near-identical evidence sitting either side of a line somebody chose.

lessons.interview_angle: Often a trap embedded in a case: they describe testing several variants and picking the winner. Naming the multiple-comparisons problem unprompted is the answer.

lessons.title: Regression: what a coefficient actually says
lessons.hook: Regression is the workhorse of analysis and the most confidently misread output in it. A coefficient is a conditional, estimated, associational quantity, and dropping any of those three words is where the trouble starts.
objectives: Interpret a coefficient in a sentence that is actually true
Name the assumptions and what breaks when they fail
Explain why adding a variable changes the others
key_points: A coefficient estimates the average change in the outcome per unit change in that predictor, holding the other predictors in the model fixed.
'Holding the others fixed' is doing enormous work. Add or remove a variable and the remaining coefficients change, sometimes sign included.
Each coefficient is an estimate with a standard error. Reporting it without that is reporting a point where you have a distribution.
R-squared is the share of variance explained. It always rises when you add predictors, which is why adjusted R-squared exists and why neither measures whether the model is right.
The usual assumptions are linearity in the parameters, independent errors, constant error variance and no perfect collinearity. Residual plots are how you check rather than assume.
Correlated predictors inflate standard errors and make individual coefficients unstable, even while overall prediction stays fine.
Logistic regression models the log-odds of a binary outcome; its coefficients are not probabilities and exponentiating gives an odds ratio, not a risk ratio.
Regression describes association. Causal reading requires an experimental design or an identification strategy, not a bigger dataset.

example.caption: A coefficient that flips
example.body: Regress loan default on FICO band alone and the coefficient is large. Add loan-to-value and it shrinks; add product type and it can move again. Nothing about the borrowers changed. The first model was attributing to FICO everything correlated with it, because 'holding the others fixed' held nothing fixed when there were no others. This is why 'controlling for' is a claim about a specific model, not a property of the world.

misconceptions.claim: A high R-squared means a good model.
misconceptions.correction: It measures fit to the data you have. An overfitted model has excellent R-squared and no predictive value, and a well-specified model of a noisy process can have a low one.

misconceptions.claim: A significant coefficient means that variable matters.
misconceptions.correction: It means it is distinguishable from zero in this specification. Change the covariates and the answer can change.

misconceptions.claim: Logistic regression coefficients are probabilities.
misconceptions.correction: They are on the log-odds scale. Converting to a probability depends on the values of every other predictor.

lessons.interview_angle: 'Walk me through a model you built' — and your Omnicals regression forecast will get this question. Be ready on how you validated it and what you did when it missed.

lessons.title: Experiments: the only clean route to cause
lessons.hook: Randomisation is what licenses the word 'caused'. Everything else in experiment design exists to protect that one property from the ways real systems break it.
objectives: Design a test with the decision made before the data
Compute what sample size a given effect needs
Name the ways randomisation gets broken in practice
key_points: Random assignment makes the groups exchangeable in expectation, so any systematic difference in outcome is attributable to the treatment. That is the whole argument.
Fix the metric, the threshold and the sample size before starting. Deciding afterwards converts a test into a search for a result.
Power analysis says what sample size is needed to detect an effect of a given size. Running an underpowered test wastes the traffic and produces an uninterpretable null.
The minimum detectable effect is a business decision: below some size the change is not worth shipping, and there is no point powering to detect it.
The randomisation unit must match the interference. Randomising by session when users see both variants leaks the treatment and biases the comparison toward zero.
Novelty and primacy effects mean early results often differ from steady state, which is one reason a fixed horizon beats stopping when it looks good.
Sanity checks come before analysis: did the split actually come out near 50/50, are the groups balanced on pre-treatment covariates, did instrumentation fire equally.
A guardrail metric protects against winning on the target metric while damaging something you care about more.

example.caption: Why a session-level split can hide a real effect
example.body: You test a new application flow, randomising by session. A borrower starts on their phone in the old flow, finishes on a laptop in the new one, and their outcome lands in whichever bucket the last session fell in. Both arms are now contaminated with each other's experience, the measured difference shrinks toward zero, and a genuine improvement reads as no effect. Randomising by borrower costs nothing and removes it.

misconceptions.claim: You can stop the test as soon as it hits significance.
misconceptions.correction: Repeatedly testing as data arrives inflates the false positive rate substantially. Fix the horizon, or use a method designed for sequential looks.

misconceptions.claim: An A/A test is a waste of traffic.
misconceptions.correction: It validates the whole apparatus. If an A/A test shows a significant difference, your instrumentation or assignment is broken and every result is suspect.

lessons.interview_angle: 'How would you test this change' is a standard product-analyst question. Metric, unit of randomisation, sample size, guardrails, horizon — in that order.

lessons.title: Causality without an experiment
lessons.hook: Most questions worth answering cannot be randomised. Knowing which of those you can still answer, and saying plainly when you cannot, is most of what senior analytical judgement is.
objectives: Distinguish a confounder from a mediator from a collider
Say why 'controlling for everything' is not a strategy
Choose language that matches the evidence
key_points: A confounder causes both the treatment and the outcome, and leaving it out biases the estimate. Adjusting for it helps.
A mediator sits on the causal path between treatment and outcome. Adjusting for it removes part of the very effect you are trying to measure.
A collider is caused by both. Adjusting for it creates a spurious association between things that were independent — which is why adding controls can make an estimate worse.
It follows that you cannot decide what to control for from the data alone. It requires a claim about the causal structure, which is an assumption you should state.
Selection into the sample is a collider you did not choose. Studying only funded loans, or only customers who replied, conditions on an outcome and distorts everything downstream.
Quasi-experimental designs — difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity, instrumental variables — each buy identification with a specific assumption that is worth naming out loud.
When none of that is available, 'associated with' is the honest phrase, and using it is a mark of seniority rather than weakness.

example.caption: Controlling for a mediator, and destroying the finding
example.body: A new underwriting tool is meant to reduce time-to-close. You regress close time on tool usage and control for number of document requests — and the effect disappears. The tool worked *by* reducing document requests. Controlling for the mechanism removed the effect from the estimate, and the conclusion 'no impact' is exactly backwards. Nothing in the data would have told you; only knowing what the tool does.

misconceptions.claim: Add every available control to be safe.
misconceptions.correction: Controlling for mediators removes real effects and controlling for colliders manufactures fake ones. More controls is not more rigour.

misconceptions.claim: A large enough dataset settles causation.
misconceptions.correction: Size reduces noise, not confounding. A million rows of observational data has the same identification problem as a thousand.

lessons.interview_angle: Senior analyst and product-analyst loops probe this deliberately: 'usage correlates with retention, what do you conclude'. The wanted answer includes what you would need to say more.

lessons.title: Framing a problem, and the leak that ruins it
lessons.hook: Most failed models are not badly tuned. They answer a question nobody asked, or they were tested on information that will not exist when they run.
objectives: Turn a business question into a supervised learning problem
Split data so the score means something
Recognise leakage before it flatters you
key_points: Supervised learning needs three things stated before any modelling: what one row is, what is being predicted, and at what moment in time the prediction is made.
The prediction time matters most. Every feature must be computable from information available at that moment, or the model cannot be used.
Data leakage is using information at training time that will not exist at prediction time. It produces excellent test scores and a model that fails immediately in production.
Common leaks: a field updated after the outcome, an aggregate computed over the whole dataset including the test rows, or an identifier that encodes the label.
The split must mirror the deployment. Time-ordered data needs a time-based split — random folds let the model train on the future and test on the past.
Three sets, not two: train to fit, validation to choose, test to report once. Choosing on the test set turns it into a validation set and the reported score into an optimistic one.
A baseline comes first. Predicting the majority class, or last month's value, is often surprisingly hard to beat and tells you whether the problem is worth modelling.

example.caption: The feature that was updated after the fact
example.body: A model predicting loan delinquency includes 'number of collection calls'. It scores beautifully. It is also useless: collection calls happen because the loan went delinquent, so the feature encodes the answer. At prediction time — when you want to know which current loans will go bad — that field is zero for every one of them. The score was measuring how well the model could read the future, and it could read it perfectly, because you handed it to it.

misconceptions.claim: A high test score means the model will work.
misconceptions.correction: Only if the test set resembles deployment. Leakage and a mis-specified split are both invisible in the score and fatal in production.

misconceptions.claim: Random splits are fine for any data.
misconceptions.correction: For time-ordered data they train on the future. The realistic split is by time, and it usually lowers the score — which is the point.

lessons.interview_angle: 'Your model does great offline and badly in production — why' is a standard question and leakage is the first thing to name.

lessons.title: Bias, variance, and what regularisation buys
lessons.hook: Every knob on every model trades the same two things against each other. Once you can name which one you are currently paying for, tuning stops being guesswork.
objectives: Diagnose underfitting versus overfitting from a learning curve
Explain what a regularisation penalty does
Choose a remedy that matches the diagnosis
key_points: Expected error decomposes into bias — error from a model too simple to represent the pattern — variance — error from a model so flexible it changes with the sample — and irreducible noise.
The diagnosis is the gap between training and validation performance. Both poor means high bias; training far better than validation means high variance.
The remedies are opposite. High bias wants more capacity, better features, less regularisation. High variance wants more data, less capacity, more regularisation.
Regularisation adds a penalty on the size of the coefficients, so the fit has to earn its complexity. L2 shrinks coefficients smoothly; L1 drives some to exactly zero and so selects features.
Cross-validation estimates out-of-sample performance more stably than one split, which matters most when data is scarce.
Early stopping is regularisation for iterative learners: stop when validation error starts rising rather than when training error stops falling.
More data reduces variance and does nothing for bias. If the model is too simple, collecting more rows will not help.

example.caption: Reading the gap
example.body: Training accuracy 0.98, validation 0.71. That gap is variance — the model memorised. Now training 0.72, validation 0.70. Almost no gap, and both poor: that is bias, and adding data or regularisation will do nothing at all. Same two numbers, opposite prescriptions, and reading them the wrong way round is how people spend a week tuning in the wrong direction.

misconceptions.claim: More data always helps.
misconceptions.correction: It reduces variance. Against a high-bias model it changes nothing, and the time is better spent on features or capacity.

misconceptions.claim: Regularisation is a way to improve accuracy.
misconceptions.correction: It trades training fit for generalisation. On an underfitted model it makes everything worse.

lessons.interview_angle: 'Your model underperforms, what do you check' — the expected answer is the train/validation gap and what it implies, not a list of algorithms to try.

lessons.title: Metrics: which mistake are you willing to make
lessons.hook: A classifier does not output a class, it outputs a score. Choosing the threshold is a business decision wearing a technical costume, and accuracy hides it entirely.
objectives: Choose a metric that matches the cost of each error
Read a confusion matrix and a ROC curve
Say why accuracy misleads on imbalanced data
key_points: The confusion matrix is the ground truth: true and false positives, true and false negatives. Every metric is a summary of it, and summaries lose things.
Precision is the share of predicted positives that were right. Recall is the share of actual positives that were found. Moving the threshold trades one for the other.
Accuracy is misleading whenever classes are imbalanced: at 1% fraud, predicting 'never fraud' is 99% accurate and worthless.
The F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, useful when you need a single number and the two matter roughly equally — which is often not true.
ROC-AUC summarises performance across all thresholds and is insensitive to class balance. Precision-recall AUC is more informative when positives are rare.
For most decisions the threshold matters more than the model. Two models with identical AUC can behave completely differently at the operating point you actually use.
For regression, MAE treats every error equally and RMSE punishes large ones more. Which you want depends on whether one big miss is worse than several small ones.

example.caption: Same model, two businesses
example.body: A delinquency model scores every loan. Set the threshold low and you catch nearly every bad loan and flood the servicing team with false alarms — right, if a review costs ten minutes and a missed default costs thousands. Set it high and you only flag the near-certain ones — right, if flagging triggers something the borrower experiences. The model is identical. The threshold is the entire decision, and it is not a modelling choice.

misconceptions.claim: A 95% accurate model is a good model.
misconceptions.correction: Compare it to the base rate first. If 95% of cases are negative, it may have learned nothing at all.

misconceptions.claim: AUC tells you how the model will perform.
misconceptions.correction: It averages over thresholds you will never use. Performance at your operating point is the number that matters.

lessons.interview_angle: 'Which metric would you use and why' is asked constantly and answered badly. Tie it to the cost of each error type in that specific business.

lessons.title: Trees and ensembles: why they win on tabular data
lessons.hook: For tabular business data, gradient-boosted trees beat neural networks more often than not, and understanding why tells you a lot about what your data actually is.
objectives: Explain how a decision tree splits
Distinguish bagging from boosting
Say when a linear model is still the better choice
key_points: A decision tree splits the data repeatedly on the feature and threshold that best separates the target, producing rules that are readable in isolation.
A single deep tree overfits badly — it can carve out a leaf for nearly every row — which is why trees are almost always used in ensembles.

Bagging trains many trees on bootstrap samples and averages them. Random forests add a second randomisation, considering only a subset of features per split, which decorrelates the trees and reduces variance further.

Boosting trains trees in sequence, each fitting the errors the previous ones left. It reduces bias as well as variance and is usually stronger, at the cost of being easier to overfit and slower to train.
Trees need no feature scaling, handle non-linearity and interactions automatically, and cope with mixed types — which is most of why they dominate on tabular data.
They extrapolate badly. A tree can only predict values it saw in training, so a genuinely out-of-range input gets the nearest leaf rather than a trend continued.
Feature importance from trees is easily misread: correlated features split their importance between them, and importance is not causal.
A linear model is still preferable when the relationship really is linear, when coefficients must be explained to a regulator, or when data is small.

example.caption: Why the tree found the interaction and the regression did not
example.body: Default risk is higher for high loan-to-value borrowers, but only in one product. A linear model with both variables sees two independent effects and misses that; you would have to know to add the interaction term yourself. A tree splits on product, then splits on LTV inside one branch and not the other — it discovered the interaction because that is what splitting does. That is the tabular advantage in one sentence.

misconceptions.claim: Random forests and gradient boosting are basically the same.
misconceptions.correction: Bagging averages independent trees to cut variance. Boosting fits residuals in sequence to cut bias. They fail in different ways and tune differently.

misconceptions.claim: Feature importance shows what drives the outcome.
misconceptions.correction: It shows what the model used. Correlated features share importance arbitrarily, and none of it is causal.

lessons.interview_angle: 'Why did you pick that model' — for tabular data the honest answer is usually gradient boosting, and being able to say why beats naming the fanciest option.

lessons.title: Rare events, and how not to fool yourself
lessons.hook: Fraud, default and churn are all rare, and rarity breaks the defaults. Every technique for handling it also distorts something, and knowing which is the skill.
objectives: Say why imbalance is a problem for training and for evaluation separately
Compare resampling with class weights
Explain why resampling breaks probability calibration
key_points: Imbalance causes two distinct problems: the learner sees too few positives to characterise them, and the usual metrics stop being informative.
Oversampling the minority risks memorising the few positives. Undersampling the majority throws away real information. Both change the class balance the model learns.
SMOTE creates synthetic minority examples by interpolating between neighbours rather than copying, which reduces exact memorisation but can invent implausible combinations.
Class weights penalise minority errors more without changing the data, and are usually the first thing to try because nothing is fabricated or discarded.

Any resampling changes the base rate the model implicitly learns, so its predicted probabilities no longer match reality. If you need calibrated probabilities, recalibrate afterwards or use weights instead.
Resample only the training data. Touching the validation or test set makes the evaluation measure a world that does not exist.
Precision-recall curves are more informative than ROC when positives are rare, because ROC's false positive rate has a huge denominator and moves very little.

example.caption: The 2% problem
example.body: Two percent of loans go delinquent. Train without adjustment and the model can score 98% accuracy by never predicting delinquency — and its ranking may still be useful, which is why you look at the scores rather than the classes. Oversample to 50/50 and the model now believes delinquency is a coin flip: its predicted probabilities are wildly overstated, and if anyone downstream uses them as expected loss, every number is wrong. The ranking improved and the probabilities became lies.

misconceptions.claim: Always balance the classes before training.
misconceptions.correction: It is one option with a real cost. Class weights often work as well and leave probabilities interpretable.

misconceptions.claim: Resampling the whole dataset is fine as long as you are consistent.
misconceptions.correction: Resampling the test set means measuring performance on a distribution that will never occur.

lessons.interview_angle: Any fraud, risk or churn role asks this. Mentioning that resampling breaks calibration is the detail that signals you have deployed one.

lessons.title: After deployment: drift, monitoring and decay
lessons.hook: A model is not finished when it ships. It is a component whose accuracy decays silently while everything around it keeps returning numbers.
objectives: Distinguish data drift from concept drift
Design monitoring that detects failure before users do
Say why a model can degrade with no code change
key_points: Data drift is the input distribution changing. Concept drift is the relationship between inputs and outcome changing. Both degrade the model and they need different responses.
Drift happens without any change to your code, because the world moves — new products, new segments, a rate change, a competitor.
Monitor inputs as well as outputs. Feature distributions shift before performance does, which is what makes them an early warning rather than a post-mortem.
Ground truth is usually delayed. You learn whether a loan defaulted months later, so proxy metrics — score distribution, prediction rate, feature ranges — have to carry the monitoring in between.
A prediction-distribution shift with unchanged inputs usually means a pipeline break, not a model problem. That is the cheapest and most common cause.
Retraining on a schedule is a blunt instrument. Retraining on a trigger — a drift threshold or a performance drop — is better, and needs the monitoring to exist first.
Log the inputs and the prediction for every call. Without that you cannot debug a bad decision after the fact, and someone will eventually ask you to.

example.caption: The model that broke because an upstream default changed
example.body: Someone changes a source system so a missing income field arrives as 0 instead of null. The pipeline does not error. The model does not error. It just starts scoring a slice of applicants as if they earned nothing, and the only symptom is a quiet shift in the score distribution. Output monitoring catches this in a day; waiting for ground truth catches it in a quarter.

misconceptions.claim: If accuracy is stable, the model is fine.
misconceptions.correction: Accuracy needs labels, which arrive late. By the time it moves you have been making bad decisions for however long the label delay is.

misconceptions.claim: Drift means retrain.
misconceptions.correction: Check for a pipeline break first — it is more common, cheaper to fix, and retraining on broken data bakes the break in.

lessons.interview_angle: 'How would you know if your model stopped working' separates people who have shipped from people who have trained. Naming label delay and proxy monitoring is the answer.

lessons.title: Complexity: why the slow version is slow
lessons.hook: You do not need to compute Big-O to write good analysis code. You need to notice when a loop is inside another loop over the same data, because that is when a job that ran in seconds starts running overnight.
objectives: Read Big-O as a growth rate rather than a speed
Recognise the accidental nested loop
Pick the data structure that removes it
key_points: Big-O describes how work grows with input size, not how fast something runs. An O(n^2) algorithm can beat an O(n log n) one on small inputs and lose catastrophically on large ones.
The common shapes: O(1) constant, O(log n) halving, O(n) linear, O(n log n) a good sort, O(n^2) every pair.
A list membership test is O(n) — Python scans it. A set or dict lookup is O(1) on average, because it hashes straight to the slot.
That single swap is the most valuable optimisation in ordinary data work: a lookup inside a loop turns O(n^2) into O(n).
Appending to a list is amortised O(1); inserting at the front is O(n) because everything shifts. A deque is the structure for both ends.
Sorting is O(n log n) and is often worth doing once to make everything afterwards cheaper, rather than searching repeatedly.
Memory has a complexity too. Building a list of a million dictionaries to then aggregate is a memory decision as much as a time one.

example.caption: The reconciliation that took four hours
example.body: For each of 50,000 ledger rows, check whether its id appears in a list of 50,000 expected ids. That is 2.5 billion comparisons, and it is the shape of nearly every accidentally slow script — a loop, and inside it a scan over something else. Convert the expected ids to a set once, up front, and each check becomes a hash lookup. Same logic, same output, 50,000 operations instead of 2.5 billion.

misconceptions.claim: Big-O tells you which code is faster.
misconceptions.correction: It tells you how each scales. Constants and cache behaviour decide small inputs, and they can dominate entirely.

misconceptions.claim: `in` is a cheap operator.
misconceptions.correction: Its cost depends entirely on what is on the right. On a list it scans; on a set it hashes.

lessons.interview_angle: Rarely asked directly in analyst interviews, and constantly asked indirectly: 'this job takes six hours, what would you look at'.

lessons.title: pandas: grain, merge, and the index that bites
lessons.hook: pandas is SQL with an extra concept — the index — and most confusing behaviour comes from that concept doing something you did not ask for.
objectives: State a DataFrame's grain and keep track of it through a merge
Choose between merge, join and concat deliberately
Say what the index is doing to your operation
key_points: A DataFrame has a grain exactly like a table does, and merge changes it exactly like a join does. The one-to-many fan-out is the same bug in a different language.
The index is a labelled axis, not just row numbers. Operations align on it silently, which is powerful and is why arithmetic between two Series can produce NaNs where you expected numbers.
merge joins on columns; join defaults to joining on the index; concat stacks along an axis without matching keys. Reaching for the wrong one produces confidently wrong shapes.
Always check the row count before and after a merge. `validate='one_to_one'` or `'one_to_many'` makes pandas raise instead of silently duplicating.
groupby collapses to the grain of the grouping keys, like GROUP BY. transform returns a value per original row instead, which is the pandas equivalent of a window function.
Chained assignment — `df[df.a > 1]['b'] = 0` — may write to a temporary copy and silently do nothing. Use `.loc` for assignment.
NaN is not equal to itself, so filtering with `!= value` drops NaN rows exactly as SQL's three-valued logic does.

example.caption: The merge that quietly tripled the totals
example.body: Merge a loans frame onto a payments frame and sum the principal. The number is three times too big and nothing errored — every loan's principal was repeated once per payment. This is the SQL grain lesson in pandas clothing, and the fix is the same: aggregate to loan grain first, or pass `validate='one_to_one'` and let it raise rather than compute.

misconceptions.claim: merge and join are interchangeable.
misconceptions.correction: join uses the index by default and merge uses columns. Mixing them up joins on the wrong thing and often still returns rows.

misconceptions.claim: A SettingWithCopyWarning is noise.
misconceptions.correction: It is telling you the write may have gone to a copy. Sometimes it did, and your change silently vanished.

lessons.interview_angle: Take-homes are usually pandas. The reviewable signal is whether you checked shape after a merge and handled nulls deliberately.

lessons.title: Vectorisation: stop writing the loop
lessons.hook: A loop over a DataFrame is usually a hundred times slower than the vectorised form, and the vectorised form is usually shorter. This is the rare case where fast and readable are the same code.
objectives: Replace an apply or iterrows with a vectorised expression
Say why vectorised operations are faster
Know when a loop is genuinely the right answer
key_points: Vectorised operations push the loop into compiled code operating over contiguous memory, avoiding per-row Python object overhead.
iterrows is the slowest common pattern: it builds a Series object per row. apply is better but still calls a Python function per row.
Boolean masks replace conditional loops: `df.loc[df.status == 'delinquent', 'flag'] = 1` touches every matching row in one operation.
np.where and np.select express if/else and multi-branch logic across a whole column at once.
Categorical dtypes cut memory dramatically for repeated strings, which matters more than speed once frames get large.
Vectorisation trades memory for speed — it materialises intermediate arrays. On a frame near your memory limit, chunking may beat it.
A loop is right when each iteration depends on the last, or when the work per row is genuinely complex. Recognising that is not a failure to vectorise.

example.caption: Same logic, two orders of magnitude
example.body: Flagging delinquent loans with `for i, row in df.iterrows(): ...` constructs a Series for every row and calls back into Python each time. `df['flag'] = (df.paid_at.isna()). astype(int)` does the whole column in one compiled pass. On a few hundred rows neither matters. On a million the first is a coffee break and the second is instant, and the second is also less code.

misconceptions.claim: apply is vectorised.
misconceptions.correction: It is a loop with nicer syntax. It calls your Python function once per row.

misconceptions.claim: Vectorised is always better.
misconceptions.correction: It builds intermediates. Near a memory ceiling, or with genuinely sequential logic, chunking or a loop wins.

lessons.interview_angle: Shows up in take-home review rather than as a question. Vectorised code reads as someone who has processed real volumes.

lessons.title: Making analysis code trustworthy
lessons.hook: Analysis code has a specific failure mode: it runs, produces a number, and the number is wrong. Nothing crashes. The habits that catch that are cheap and mostly unglamorous.
objectives: Add assertions that catch a wrong answer, not just a crash
Make a result reproducible by someone else
Say what belongs in a test for a data pipeline
key_points: Assert the shape of your data at each step: expected row count, no unexpected nulls, keys unique where they should be. A pipeline that fails loudly beats one that returns a plausible number.
Reconciliation is the strongest check available in analysis: totals tie to a known source, counts match upstream, a sum by segment equals the overall sum.
Pin dependencies. An analysis that produced a number last quarter and cannot reproduce it today is not evidence of anything.
Set random seeds wherever sampling or model fitting happens, or the number changes between runs and nobody can tell whether a change is real.
Test the transformation functions, not the notebook. A function taking a frame and returning a frame is testable with a five-row fixture; a notebook is not.
The tests worth writing are the edge cases that produce silent wrongness: empty input, all-null column, duplicate keys, a single row.
Separate extraction from transformation. Code that fetches and transforms in one function can only be tested with a live connection, so it will not be tested.

example.caption: The assertion that would have caught it
example.body: One line after a merge — `assert len(df) == len(loans), f'grain changed: {len(df)} vs {len(loans)}'` — turns the most common silent error in analysis into an immediate, specific failure. It costs nothing to write, it documents the intended grain for the next reader, and it fails at the moment the mistake happens rather than three steps later in a total that merely looks high.

misconceptions.claim: Analysis code does not need tests.
misconceptions.correction: It needs them more than most code, because its failure mode is a wrong number rather than an exception. Nothing else will catch that.

misconceptions.claim: It ran without errors, so it is correct.
misconceptions.correction: Every silent data bug ran without errors. That is the definition of the category.

lessons.interview_angle: 'How do you know your analysis is right' is a seniority question. Reconciliation and assertions are the answer; 'I check it carefully' is not.

lessons.title: Normalisation, and when to stop
lessons.hook: Normalisation exists to stop the same fact being stored twice, because two copies eventually disagree. Analytical modelling then deliberately breaks it, and knowing why is the whole subject.
objectives: Explain what an update anomaly is
Describe third normal form in a sentence
Say why warehouses denormalise on purpose
key_points: Normalisation organises tables so each fact is stored once. The point is to prevent anomalies, where updating a fact in one place leaves a stale copy elsewhere.
First normal form: no repeating groups, one value per cell. Second: no partial dependency on part of a composite key. Third: no attribute depending on another non-key attribute.
In practice, third normal form means every column describes the key, the whole key and nothing but the key.
Transactional systems normalise because they are write-heavy and correctness under concurrent updates is the priority.
Analytical systems denormalise because they are read-heavy: joins cost time on every query, storage is cheap, and the data is loaded rather than updated in place.
The denormalised copy is safe precisely because it is derived. It is rebuilt from the normalised source, so a disagreement is a pipeline bug rather than a permanent inconsistency.
Choosing a shape means naming the workload. Neither form is correct in the abstract.

example.caption: The address stored twice
