example.body: Put the borrower's address on every loan row and one borrower moving means updating every one of their loans. Miss one and you now have two addresses for one person, with nothing to say which is right. That is an update anomaly, and it is the entire argument for normalisation. In a warehouse the same duplication is fine — because nobody updates it in place, and the whole table is rebuilt from the source that does store it once.

misconceptions.claim: Normalised is correct and denormalised is lazy.
misconceptions.correction: They optimise for different workloads. A star schema is a deliberate denormalisation, not a mistake.

misconceptions.claim: More normalisation is always safer.
misconceptions.correction: Past third normal form the gains are usually theoretical and the join cost is real.

lessons.interview_angle: 'Walk me through how you would model this' expects the workload to be named before the shape is chosen.

lessons.title: Facts, dimensions, and stating the grain
lessons.hook: Dimensional modelling is a small vocabulary that makes analytical databases predictable — and almost every wrong number in one comes from skipping its first step.
objectives: Separate facts from dimensions in a new domain
State a fact table's grain before designing it
Explain why a star beats a snowflake for analysis
key_points: A fact table holds measurements — things you sum, count or average — at a stated grain. A dimension table holds the descriptive attributes you filter and group by.
Declaring the grain is the first step and the one people skip: 'one row per payment', not 'payments'. Every subsequent decision depends on it.
Facts are numeric and additive where possible. A fact that cannot be summed across a dimension — a ratio, a percentage — is a warning sign; store the numerator and denominator instead.
A star schema keeps dimensions denormalised and one join from the fact. A snowflake normalises them into chains, saving space and costing joins on every query.
Conformed dimensions are shared across fact tables, which is what lets two different processes be compared on the same customer or the same date.
Mixing grains in one fact table is the classic error — order headers and order lines together — and it makes every aggregate ambiguous.
A date dimension is worth building rather than deriving, because fiscal periods, holidays and week definitions are business facts that do not follow from a timestamp.

example.caption: Two facts, two grains, one mistake
example.body: Loan originations and loan payments are different processes measured at different grains, and putting them in one table forces a row to be either a loan with null payment columns or a payment with repeated loan columns. Either way every SUM needs a filter nobody will remember to write. Two fact tables sharing a conformed borrower and date dimension answers both questions and can still be joined when someone asks a question spanning them.

misconceptions.claim: Star schemas are outdated now that storage is cheap.
misconceptions.correction: The shape exists for query predictability and comprehension, not storage. It is still the default in modern warehouses.

misconceptions.claim: Grain is obvious from the table name.
misconceptions.correction: 'payments' could be one row per payment, per scheduled instalment, or per payment attempt. Only stating it removes the ambiguity.

lessons.interview_angle: Analytics-engineering interviews are largely this. Say the grain out loud first, every time.

lessons.title: History: what happens when an attribute changes
lessons.hook: A customer moves city. Overwrite the old value and last year's report quietly changes. That single decision is what slowly changing dimensions are about.
objectives: Choose an SCD type for a given attribute
Explain why Type 1 makes old reports irreproducible
Write a query that gets the value as of a date
key_points: A slowly changing dimension is one whose descriptive attributes change over time. The type describes what happens to the previous value.
Type 1 overwrites. Simple, and it silently rewrites history — every report that grouped by the old value now reports differently.
Type 2 adds a new row with valid-from and valid-to dates and a current flag, preserving history at the cost of a dimension that grows and joins that need a date predicate.
Type 3 keeps a 'previous value' column, which handles exactly one change and is rarely the right answer.
The choice is a business question: does anyone need to reproduce last year's report exactly, or is the current value always what is meant.
With Type 2 the fact must join on the surrogate key valid at the transaction date, not on the natural key, or every historical row picks up today's attributes.
Auditability usually forces Type 2 in regulated domains, because 'what did we believe at the time' is a question someone will eventually have to answer.

example.caption: The report that changed after it was signed
example.body: A borrower's risk band is corrected from B to A. With Type 1 the dimension is overwritten, and the delinquency-by-risk-band report for last quarter now shows different numbers than the copy that was signed off — with no record of why. With Type 2 the old row stays, closed off at the change date, and the historical report reproduces exactly while today's reporting uses the current row.

misconceptions.claim: Type 2 everything to be safe.
misconceptions.correction: It multiplies dimension rows and complicates every join. Use it where history is genuinely needed and Type 1 where the current value is always meant.

misconceptions.claim: A current-flag column is enough for history.
misconceptions.correction: It tells you which row is current, not which was current on a given date. Reproducing an old report needs the valid-from and valid-to range.

lessons.interview_angle: A near-guaranteed question in analytics engineering. Naming the audit implication rather than only the mechanics is what distinguishes an answer.

lessons.title: Metric definitions, and where they should live
lessons.hook: Two dashboards showing different revenue for the same month is the most common failure in analytics, and it is never a data problem. It is two people having written the definition twice.
objectives: Say why a metric defined in three dashboards is three metrics
Describe what a semantic layer does
Design a metric that survives being asked about
key_points: A metric is a definition, not a number: what is counted, at what grain, over which population, with which filters and which time basis.
When each dashboard implements the definition itself, the definitions drift, and the disagreement surfaces in a meeting rather than in a test.
A semantic layer defines metrics once, above the tables and below the dashboards, so every consumer resolves the same definition.
The definition must state the time basis explicitly — booked date versus recognised date versus paid date produce different and equally defensible revenue numbers.
A metric tree decomposes a headline number into the factors that drive it, so a movement can be attributed rather than merely observed.
Ownership matters as much as definition. A metric with no owner is one nobody may change, and therefore one everyone quietly forks.
Changing a definition changes history. Version it and say when it changed, or a step in the chart gets blamed on the business.

example.caption: Three revenue numbers, all correct
example.body: Finance counts revenue when it is recognised. Sales counts it when the deal is booked. The ops dashboard counts it when cash arrives. All three are right, all three differ, and every meeting starts by relitigating whose number is real. The fix is not choosing a winner — it is naming all three, defining each once, and labelling every chart with which one it shows.

misconceptions.claim: Everyone knows what revenue means.
misconceptions.correction: Everyone knows what it means to them. The disagreement is invisible until two numbers meet.

misconceptions.claim: A semantic layer is a BI tool feature.
misconceptions.correction: It is a discipline about where definitions live. A well-run dbt project with tested metric models is one.

lessons.interview_angle: 'Two dashboards disagree, what do you do' — the answer is to compare the definitions before comparing the data.

lessons.title: ETL, ELT, and where the transform belongs
lessons.hook: The letters describe one decision: do you clean the data before it lands or after. That choice decides what you can recover from when a transformation turns out to be wrong.
objectives: Choose between ETL and ELT for a given constraint
Explain why keeping raw data is a recoverability decision
Say when ETL is still right
key_points: ETL transforms in a dedicated step and loads the result. ELT loads raw data into the destination and transforms it there using the warehouse's own compute.
ELT became the default because warehouse compute got cheap and elastic, so the transformation step no longer needed its own infrastructure.
The decisive argument is recoverability. ELT keeps the raw data, so a transformation bug is re-runnable; under ETL the untransformed data was never stored and the mistake is permanent.
ETL still wins where raw data must not land in the destination at all — regulated fields, secrets, anything the destination is not cleared to hold.
A staging layer holding raw-as-landed data is what makes ELT recoverable. Transforming straight into the presentation layer gives up the benefit while keeping the shape.
Layering — raw, then cleaned and conformed, then presentation — makes each step testable and lets a failure be traced to a stage rather than a pipeline.
Incremental loads process only what changed. They are much cheaper and much easier to get subtly wrong than full refreshes.

example.caption: The bug you can and cannot recover from
example.body: A currency conversion is applied with the wrong rate for a week. Under ELT the raw amounts are still in staging: fix the transformation, re-run, done. Under ETL the converted values are all you ever stored, the original amounts are gone, and there is no way back except re-extracting from a source that may itself have moved on. Same bug, one afternoon versus a data-loss incident.

misconceptions.claim: ELT is just ETL with the steps reordered.
misconceptions.correction: Reordering is what preserves the raw data, which changes what is recoverable. That is the substance, not the sequence.

misconceptions.claim: Incremental is always better than full refresh.
misconceptions.correction: Incremental has to handle late-arriving and deleted records correctly. A full refresh is often the right choice until volume forces the issue.

lessons.interview_angle: 'Walk me through a pipeline you built' — your Supreme Lending pipeline answers this. Say which shape it was and why.

lessons.title: Retries: designing for the second run
lessons.hook: Every scheduler retries. If running your pipeline twice does not produce the same result as running it once, you have a data corruption bug waiting for a bad network day.
objectives: Say what makes an operation idempotent
Turn an append-based load into a safe one
Explain why partial failure is the hard case
key_points: An operation is idempotent when applying it more than once leaves the same end state as applying it once. That is what makes an automatic retry safe.
Appending is not idempotent: a retry after a partial failure duplicates whatever the first attempt wrote.
Upserting on a natural key is idempotent, because the second run overwrites the rows the first wrote rather than adding to them.
Replacing a whole partition is the simplest idempotent pattern in warehousing: delete the day and rewrite it, so a re-run converges regardless of what the first attempt managed.
Partial failure is the difficult case: some rows written, then a crash. Without transactions or partition replacement you cannot tell how far it got.
Side effects outside the database — emails, webhooks, file drops — are the ones retries hurt most, and they need their own deduplication key.
Backfills are just retries over a wider window. A pipeline that is safe to retry is safe to backfill, and one that is not cannot be corrected without manual cleanup.

example.caption: The day that got counted twice
example.body: A nightly job appends yesterday's payments. It times out at 90% and the scheduler retries. Now 90% of yesterday's payments exist twice, every downstream total is inflated by an amount nobody can derive, and the only fix is identifying and deleting the duplicates by hand. Replacing the partition instead — delete where date = yesterday, then insert — makes the retry a no-op regardless of where the first run died.

misconceptions.claim: Retries are rare enough not to design for.
misconceptions.correction: Every orchestrator retries by default. It is a normal operating condition, not an exception.

misconceptions.claim: A unique constraint makes it idempotent.
misconceptions.correction: It stops duplicates by making the retry fail. That is a stuck pipeline rather than a converged one — better than corruption, worse than an upsert.

lessons.interview_angle: 'What happens if this job runs twice' is a standard data-engineering probe. Naming partition replacement or upsert-by-key is the answer.

lessons.title: Testing data, not just code
lessons.hook: Code tests tell you the transformation does what you wrote. Data tests tell you the data is what you assumed — and it is the second one that fails at three in the morning.
objectives: Write the four tests that catch most breakages
Decide what should fail the pipeline versus warn
Say why freshness is a data test
key_points: The high-value tests are few: uniqueness of the key, not-null on required fields, accepted values for enums, and referential integrity to the parent table.
Row-count and volume anomaly checks catch the silent partial load, which no schema test will notice because every row present is valid.
Freshness is a data test. A table that stopped updating looks perfectly healthy to every other check, and staleness is invisible in the data itself.
Distribution checks — a mean or null rate outside its usual range — catch upstream semantic changes that keep the schema intact.
Severity is a design decision. A failed uniqueness test on a primary key should stop the pipeline; a slightly unusual distribution should warn, because blocking on it trains people to ignore alerts.
Test at the boundary where data enters your control. Failing at ingestion localises the problem to the source; failing three models later means debugging the wrong thing.
Reconciliation against an authoritative source is the strongest test available and the one most worth the effort where money is involved.

example.caption: The check that catches what schemas cannot
example.body: An upstream system changes so missing income arrives as 0 rather than null. Every row is present, every type is right, every not-null test passes, and the average income silently drops by a third. Only a distribution check notices. This is the argument for testing values and not only shapes — and it is the same failure that silently poisons a model downstream.

misconceptions.claim: Schema validation is data quality.
misconceptions.correction: It catches structural change. Semantic change — a default flipping, a unit changing — passes every schema check.

misconceptions.claim: Every failing test should stop the pipeline.
misconceptions.correction: Blocking on soft signals produces alert fatigue, and then the hard failures get ignored too.

lessons.interview_angle: 'How do you know the data is right' — your GL reconciliation and control work answers this directly. Lead with the reconciliation.

lessons.title: Incremental loading and change capture
lessons.hook: Full refreshes are simple and eventually impossible. Everything hard about the alternative comes down to three cases: updates, deletes, and things arriving late.
objectives: Choose an incremental strategy for a source
Say why deletes are the hard case
Handle late-arriving data without reprocessing everything
key_points: Incremental loading processes only records changed since the last run, identified by a watermark — usually an updated-at timestamp or an increasing id.
A timestamp watermark misses any row whose updated-at is not maintained, and silently: the row exists, it is just never picked up again.
Deletes are the fundamental problem. A source row that disappears has no updated-at, so watermark-based loads never learn about it and the warehouse keeps a record the source says is gone.
Change data capture reads the database's transaction log instead, so inserts, updates and deletes all appear as events, in order.
Late-arriving data breaks naive watermarks: a record inserted with an old timestamp lands behind the mark and is skipped forever. Overlapping windows or a lookback period are the usual mitigations.
Out-of-order events must be applied by their own timestamp rather than arrival order, or a stale update overwrites a newer value.
Full refresh remains correct and is often right. Move to incremental when volume forces it, not because it seems more sophisticated.

example.caption: The loan that stayed cancelled forever
example.body: A loan is cancelled and the row is deleted from the source. The nightly incremental load selects rows where updated_at > watermark; the deleted row has no updated_at because it no longer exists. It is never selected again, so the warehouse keeps it forever, and every count of active loans is one too high — permanently, silently, and with no error anywhere. This is why soft deletes or CDC exist.

misconceptions.claim: Incremental is strictly better than full refresh.
misconceptions.correction: It is cheaper and more complex. Correctness now depends on the source maintaining timestamps and on you handling deletes.

misconceptions.claim: CDC is just a faster incremental load.
misconceptions.correction: It carries deletes and ordering, which watermarks structurally cannot. That is a correctness difference, not a speed one.

lessons.interview_angle: 'How would you keep the warehouse in sync' — mention deletes before you are asked, because that is the part most answers miss.

lessons.title: Choosing a chart is choosing a comparison
lessons.hook: A chart type is not a style preference. It encodes a specific comparison, and the wrong encoding makes the reader do arithmetic they will get wrong.
objectives: Pick an encoding from the comparison being made
Say why pie charts and dual axes mislead
Order categories deliberately
key_points: Decide the comparison first — over time, between categories, part to whole, relationship between two measures — and the chart type follows.
People judge position along a common scale most accurately, then length, then angle, then area, then colour. Encode the most important comparison in the most accurate channel available.
Pie charts encode as angle and area, the two weakest channels, which is why comparing slices is hard and why a bar chart almost always beats one.
Bar charts must start at zero, because the bar's length is the encoding. Line charts need not, because the encoding is the slope.
Dual axes let you place any two series in any apparent relationship by choosing the scales. They imply a correlation the data may not contain.
Sort categorical bars by value rather than alphabetically unless the order is meaningful. Alphabetical order encodes nothing and hides the ranking.
Colour should carry meaning consistently — same metric, same colour, everywhere — and should not be the only channel, for readers with colour vision differences.
Direct labelling beats a legend. A legend makes the reader look away and match, every single time.

example.caption: The truncated axis
example.body: Delinquency moves from 2.1% to 2.3%. On a bar chart with the axis starting at 2.0% the second bar is three times the height of the first, and every reader takes away 'delinquency tripled'. Nothing was falsified — the numbers are printed right there — and the chart still lied, because the encoding is length and the length was made to say something the data does not.

misconceptions.claim: Always start every axis at zero.
misconceptions.correction: Bars, yes — the length is the encoding. Lines showing change over a narrow range are unreadable at zero and the slope is the encoding.

misconceptions.claim: More colour makes a chart clearer.
misconceptions.correction: Colour without meaning is decoration that competes with the data for attention.

lessons.interview_angle: Portfolio and take-home review. A chart that starts at a non-zero baseline or uses a dual axis invites exactly the question you do not want.

lessons.title: Designing backwards from the decision
lessons.hook: A dashboard nobody can name a decision for is a wall of charts. Naming the decision first is what makes everything else — which metrics, which cuts, what to remove — answerable.
objectives: Start from the decision and the person making it
Justify removing a chart
Design for the glance before the investigation
key_points: Start with the decision and its owner. 'What will someone do differently as a result of this screen' is the question that determines everything else.
Show the exception, not the state. A number that is normal needs no attention; the value of a dashboard is surfacing what is not normal.
A number without a comparison is not information. Every headline figure needs a baseline — last period, target, or same period last year.
Design for the glance first: the top of the screen answers 'is anything wrong', and detail lives below for when the answer is yes.
Every additional chart makes the others harder to see. Removing one is a real improvement, and 'someone might want it' is not a requirement.
Filters are a cost. Each one is a decision pushed onto the reader, and a sensible default beats a filter they must set correctly.
State the refresh time and the definitions on the screen. A dashboard whose freshness is unknown gets verified elsewhere, and then it is not being used.
If people export it to a spreadsheet, the dashboard failed at something specific — find out what and fix that.

example.caption: Four tabs down to one number and a list
example.body: An operations lead checked four tabs each morning to find the accounts needing attention. The replacement was one number — how many need attention today — and the list of those accounts, with everything else moved behind a link. Fewer charts, strictly less information on screen, and the morning check went from ten minutes to ten seconds, because the dashboard was finally doing the selection instead of delegating it.

misconceptions.claim: More metrics make a dashboard more useful.
misconceptions.correction: Each one competes for attention. Past a handful the reader stops scanning and starts hunting.

misconceptions.claim: Everything should be filterable.
misconceptions.correction: Filters move work onto the reader and multiply the states you must design for. Defaults are a decision you can make once.

lessons.interview_angle: Everyone claims dashboards. What distinguishes an answer is naming the decision, the person, and what you removed.

lessons.title: Delivering a finding so it lands
lessons.hook: Analysis that is right and ignored has the same effect as analysis that is wrong. How a finding is delivered is part of the work, not a soft skill bolted on after.
objectives: Lead with the answer
State uncertainty without undermining the finding
Anticipate the first question an executive will ask
key_points: Lead with the answer and the recommended action. Method belongs after, and in an appendix if it is long — the reader decides how deep to go, not you.
One message per deliverable. If there are three findings, they are three deliverables or three clearly separated sections.
State the uncertainty in terms of the decision: 'this holds unless volume drops below X' is useful, 'p = 0.04' is not, to that audience.
Name the limitation before it is found. Volunteering the weakness builds more credibility than defending it under questioning.
Quantify the so-what. 'Conversion is down 3%' becomes actionable as 'that is roughly 40 applications a month'.
Expect the first question to be 'is the data right', and have the reconciliation ready. That question is about trust rather than about data, and answering it once buys the rest of the meeting.
Write the title of the chart as the finding — 'Delinquency concentrated in one product' — rather than as a description of the axes.

example.caption: Two openings, same analysis
example.body: 'I pulled six months of data, joined it to the servicing system, and after excluding test accounts I found…' — you have lost the room before the finding. Versus: 'Delinquency is concentrated in one product, which accounts for 70% of it on 20% of volume. I would tighten that product's criteria. Here is how I checked it.' Identical work. The second one gets a decision; the first gets a follow-up meeting.

misconceptions.claim: Showing your working builds credibility.
misconceptions.correction: Showing it first buries the finding. Making it available on request is what builds credibility.

misconceptions.claim: Caveats protect you.
misconceptions.correction: Unprioritised caveats read as no confidence. Name the ones that would change the decision and drop the rest.

lessons.interview_angle: 'Tell me about an analysis that changed a decision' is asking about this directly, and the answer must include how you delivered it.

lessons.title: Data structures: choosing what to look things up in
lessons.hook: Four structures cover almost everything in ordinary engineering. Knowing what each costs is what turns a slow program into a fast one without any cleverness.
objectives: Choose between list, set, dict and deque for a task
Say what a hash table trades for O(1) lookup
Recognise when sorting first is the right move
key_points: An array or list gives O(1) access by position and O(n) search by value, because it must scan.
A hash table gives average O(1) insert and lookup by hashing the key straight to a slot. Python's dict and set are hash tables.
The trade is that hash tables are unordered, use more memory, and need hashable keys. Worst case degrades to O(n) under heavy collision.
A binary search tree keeps keys ordered, giving O(log n) lookup plus ordered traversal and range queries — which a hash table cannot do at all.
Binary search over a sorted array is O(log n) but requires the sort first. Sorting once to search many times is usually the right trade.
A queue and a stack differ only in which end you remove from, and that difference is breadth-first versus depth-first traversal.
The practical rule: if you are searching a collection inside a loop, it should almost certainly be a set or dict.

example.caption: Ordered or fast — pick one
example.body: You need to know whether an id has been seen: a set, O(1), done. You need the ids in order, or all ids between two values: a hash table cannot help you at all, and you want a sorted structure. This is the whole trade in one line — hashing destroys order to buy constant-time lookup, and if you need the order back you have to pay for it somewhere else.

misconceptions.claim: Dictionaries are unordered in Python.
misconceptions.correction: They preserve insertion order since 3.7. That is not the same as being sorted, and lookup is still by hash.

misconceptions.claim: Hash lookup is always O(1).
misconceptions.correction: It is O(1) on average. Pathological collisions degrade it, which is why hash quality matters.

lessons.interview_angle: Analyst roles rarely ask this directly and technical screens do. It is also the answer to most 'why is this script slow' questions.

lessons.title: Caching, queues and the shape of a system
lessons.hook: Two ideas explain most of how systems are made to scale: keep a copy of expensive answers, and stop making the caller wait for work that can happen later.
objectives: Say what a cache costs as well as what it saves
Explain why a queue decouples producer from consumer
Name the invalidation problem
key_points: A cache stores the result of expensive work so later requests skip it. The cost is that the copy can be stale, and knowing when to discard it is the hard part.
Cache invalidation is genuinely hard because correctness now depends on knowing every event that could change the underlying answer — and the cache is usually far from those events.
Time-based expiry trades staleness for simplicity and is right far more often than people admit. Event-based invalidation is exact and couples the cache to every writer.
A queue lets a producer hand off work and return immediately, so a slow consumer creates a backlog rather than a timeout.
That decoupling is also a durability boundary: work in a queue survives the consumer restarting, which an in-process background thread does not.
Queues change delivery guarantees. At-least-once is the common default, which means consumers must be idempotent — the same property pipelines need for retries.
Backpressure matters: an unbounded queue converts a throughput problem into a memory problem and fails later and worse.
Every cache and queue adds a place where the system can be inconsistent. Add them to solve a measured problem, not by default.

example.caption: The dashboard that showed yesterday
example.body: A dashboard query is expensive, so its result is cached for an hour. Someone corrects a record and refreshes, and the old number is still there — the cache has no idea a write happened. They refresh again, get the same number, and conclude the system is broken. Nothing is broken; the invalidation was never wired. Showing the cache timestamp on screen would have turned a bug report into a shrug.

misconceptions.claim: Caching is free performance.
misconceptions.correction: It buys speed with staleness and adds a second source of truth to keep consistent.

misconceptions.claim: A queue guarantees exactly-once delivery.
misconceptions.correction: Most give at-least-once. Exactly-once is expensive and usually approximated by making consumers idempotent.

lessons.interview_angle: System-design questions in data roles usually reduce to these two plus idempotence, which you already have from the pipelines track.
